claim: A reminder shock reinstated extinguished fear in mice, with freezing increasing from test 1 to test 2 (n = 10 mice; paired t-test, t(9) = 3.6, p = 0.0059).
source: (A) A reminder shock reinstated extinguished fear (n = 10 mice; paired t-test, t(9) = 3.6, p = 0.0059).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data showing significant increase in freezing behavior, as presented in Figure 1A.

claim: c-Fos+ cell density decreased in the infralimbic cortex (IL) with reinstatement compared to extinction (n = 8–11 mice; F(2,27) = 4.3, p = 0.023; Tukey's test, PExtinction vs Reinstatement = 0.029).
source: (C) c-Fos+ cell density decreased in the IL and the ITCv and increased in the CeM with reinstatement (n = 8–11 mice; F(2,27) = 4.3, p = 0.023 [IL]; F(2,26) = 4.8, p = 0.0016 [ITCv]; F(2,26) = 6.3, p = 0.0058 [CeM]; Tukey's test, PExtinction vs Reinstatement = 0.029 [IL], 0.035 [ITCv], 0.013 [CeM]).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data quantifying c-Fos expression in the IL across experimental groups, as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: c-Fos+ cell density decreased in the ventral intercalated amygdala neurons (ITCv) with reinstatement compared to extinction (n = 8–11 mice; F(2,26) = 4.8, p = 0.0016; Tukey's test, PExtinction vs Reinstatement = 0.035).
source: (C) c-Fos+ cell density decreased in the IL and the ITCv and increased in the CeM with reinstatement (n = 8–11 mice; F(2,27) = 4.3, p = 0.023 [IL]; F(2,26) = 4.8, p = 0.0016 [ITCv]; F(2,26) = 6.3, p = 0.0058 [CeM]; Tukey's test, PExtinction vs Reinstatement = 0.029 [IL], 0.035 [ITCv], 0.013 [CeM]).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data quantifying c-Fos expression in the ITCv across experimental groups, as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: c-Fos+ cell density increased in the medial subdivision of the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeM) with reinstatement compared to extinction (n = 8–11 mice; F(2,26) = 6.3, p = 0.0058; Tukey's test, PExtinction vs Reinstatement = 0.013).
source: (C) c-Fos+ cell density decreased in the IL and the ITCv and increased in the CeM with reinstatement (n = 8–11 mice; F(2,27) = 4.3, p = 0.023 [IL]; F(2,26) = 4.8, p = 0.0016 [ITCv]; F(2,26) = 6.3, p = 0.0058 [CeM]; Tukey's test, PExtinction vs Reinstatement = 0.029 [IL], 0.035 [ITCv], 0.013 [CeM]).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data quantifying c-Fos expression in the CeM across experimental groups, as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: IL muscimol infusions resulted in high freezing compared to vehicle (n = 10 mice; t(18) = 2.4, p = 0.030).
source: (D) IL muscimol infusions resulted in high freezing (n = 10 mice; t(18) = 2.4, p = 0.030).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from pharmacological inactivation experiments, as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Mice of the Reinstatement group showed greater freezing behaviour relative to the Extinction group (F(2,25) = 8.7, p = 0.0013; Tukey's test, PExtinction vs Reinstatement = 0.0073).
source: Mice of the Reinstatement group showed greater freezing behaviour relative to the Extinction group (F(2,25) = 8.7, p = 0.0013; Tukey's test, PFear vs Extinction = 0.0023, PExtinction vs Reinstatement = 0.0073).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data comparing freezing across experimental groups, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: IL neurons had lower miniature excitatory postsynaptic current (mEPSC) frequency in the Reinstatement group than the Extinction group (n = 8 neurons from 6 mice vs n = 8 neurons from 4 mice; F(2,21) = 3.9, p = 0.037; PExtinction vs Reinstatement = 0.030).
source: (B) IL neurons had lower mEPSC frequency in the Reinstatement group (n = 8 neurons from 6 mice) than the Extinction group (n = 8 neurons from 4 mice) (F(2,21) = 3.9, p = 0.037; PExtinction vs Reinstatement = 0.030).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recording data measuring mEPSC frequency in IL neurons, as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: mEPSC amplitude did not differ across groups (F(2,21) = 1.9, p = 0.38).
source: (C) mEPSC amplitude did not differ across groups (F(2,21) = 1.9, p = 0.38).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing no significant difference in mEPSC amplitude, as shown in Figure 2C.

claim: mEPSC frequency negatively correlated with Δfreezing (different degrees of freezing time between tests 1 and 2) in the Reinstatement group (r = −0.83, p = 0.040).
source: (D) mEPSC frequency negatively correlated with Δfreezing (different degrees of freezing time between tests 1 and 2) in the Reinstatement group (r = −0.83, p = 0.040).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between electrophysiological and behavioral measures, as shown in Figure 2D.

claim: IL neurons had a higher paired-pulse ratio (PPR) in the Reinstatement group than the Extinction group (n = 8 neurons from 5 mice vs n = 8 neurons from 4 mice; t(14) = 2.2, p = 0.049).
source: (F) IL neurons had a higher paired-pulse ratio (PPR) in the Reinstatement group (n = 8 neurons from 5 mice) than the Extinction group (n = 8 neurons from 4 mice) (t(14) = 2.2, p = 0.049).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data measuring PPR in IL neurons, as shown in Figure 2F.

claim: PPR positively correlated with Δfreezing in the Reinstatement group (r = 0.95, p = 0.012).
source: (G) PPR positively correlated with Δfreezing in the Reinstatement group (r = 0.95, p = 0.012).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between PPR and behavioral measures, as shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The maximum number of evoked spikes at any current step increased with fear extinction (F(2,58) = 4.1, p = 0.022; Tukey's test, p = 0.016) and did not change with fear reinstatement.
source: (C) The maximum number of evoked spikes at any current step increased with fear extinction (F(2,58) = 4.1, p = 0.022; Tukey's test, p = 0.016) and did not change with fear reinstatement.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data measuring intrinsic excitability of IL neurons, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Of the retrogradely labelled cells (CTBIL+) in the VTA, 59.1 ± 4.5% were immunopositive for tyrosine hydroxylase (TH+), indicating that they were dopaminergic.
source: Of the retrogradely labelled cells (CTBIL+) in the VTA, 59.1 ± 4.5% were immunopositive for a dopamine neuron marker, tyrosine hydroxylase (TH+), indicating that they were dopaminergic.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data quantifying the proportion of dopaminergic neurons among IL-projecting VTA neurons.

claim: A reminder shock increased c-Fos expression in the CTBIL+ TH+ VTA neurons (no shock: n = 7, reminder shock: n = 6 mice; t(11) = 4.3, p = 0.0012).
source: (C) A reminder shock increased the proportion of c-Fos+ neurons in IL-projecting TH+ VTA neurons (no shock: n = 7, reminder shock: n = 6 mice; t(11) = 4.3, p = 0.0012).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing increased c-Fos expression in dopaminergic VTA neurons projecting to the IL after a reminder shock, as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A reminder shock did not increase the proportion of c-Fos+ neurons in IL-projecting TH− VTA neurons (no shock: n = 7, reminder shock: n = 6 mice).
source: (D) A reminder shock did not increase the proportion of c-Fos+ neurons in IL-projecting TH− VTA neurons (no shock: n = 7, reminder shock: n = 6 mice).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing no change in c-Fos expression in non-dopaminergic VTA neurons projecting to the IL after a reminder shock, as shown in Figure 3D.

claim: SCH23390 infusions into the IL before a reminder shock suppressed reinstatement (phosphate-buffered saline [PBS]: n = 15, SCH23390: n = 14 mice; t(27) = 2.2, p = 0.039).
source: (A) SCH23390 infusions into the IL before a reminder shock suppressed reinstatement (phosphate-buffered saline [PBS]: n = 15, SCH23390: n = 14 mice; t(27) = 2.2, p = 0.039).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from pharmacological experiments blocking D1 receptors in the IL, as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SCH23390-infused mice demonstrated higher mEPSC frequency than vehicle-infused mice (n = 9, 10 neurons; t(17) = 2.2, p = 0.044).
source: (C) SCH23390-infused mice demonstrated higher mEPSC frequency (n = 9, 10 neurons; t(17) = 2.2, p = 0.044).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing that D1R blockade prevented the reduction in mEPSC frequency, as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: SCH23390 infusions had no effects on mEPSC amplitude.
source: (D) SCH23390 infusions had no effects on mEPSC amplitude.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing no effect of D1R blockade on mEPSC amplitude, as shown in Figure 4D.

claim: SCH23390-infused mice demonstrated higher c-Fos+ cell density in the ventral intercalated amygdala neurons (ITCv) compared to vehicle-infused mice (n = 7–8 mice; t(13) = 3.0, p = 0.0093).
source: (E) SCH23390-infused mice demonstrated higher and lower c-Fos+ cell density in the ventral intercalated amygdala neurons (ITCv) and the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeM), respectively (n = 7–8 mice; ITCv: t(13) = 3.0, p = 0.0093; CeM: t(14) = 2.9, p = 0.011).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing that D1R blockade prevented the decrease in ITCv c-Fos expression, as shown in Figure 4E.

claim: SCH23390-infused mice demonstrated lower c-Fos+ cell density in the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeM) compared to vehicle-infused mice (n = 7–8 mice; t(14) = 2.9, p = 0.011).
source: (E) SCH23390-infused mice demonstrated higher and lower c-Fos+ cell density in the ventral intercalated amygdala neurons (ITCv) and the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeM), respectively (n = 7–8 mice; ITCv: t(13) = 3.0, p = 0.0093; CeM: t(14) = 2.9, p = 0.011).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing that D1R blockade prevented the increase in CeM c-Fos expression, as shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Freezing time was comparable between tests 1 and 2 if mice were exposed to chamber B without a reminder shock on Day 4 (39.5 ± 4.2% in test 1 and 32.6 ± 5.3% in test 2, n = 4).
source: Freezing time was comparable between tests 1 and 2 if mice were exposed to chamber B without a reminder shock on Day 4 (39.5 ± 4.2% in test 1 and 32.6 ± 5.3% in test 2, n = 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from control experiments without reminder shock.

claim: When given the reminder shock to naive mice, the reminder shock alone did not induce high fear responses (6.0 ± 2.1%, n = 5).
source: When we gave the reminder shock to naive mice, the reminder shock alone did not induce high fear responses (6.0 ± 2.1%, n = 5), indicating that the reminder shock-induced increase in freezing was derived from the original conditioned fear, not from new learning.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from control experiments with naive mice.

claim: The reminder shock-induced increase in freezing was derived from the original conditioned fear, not from new learning.
source: When we gave the reminder shock to naive mice, the reminder shock alone did not induce high fear responses (6.0 ± 2.1%, n = 5), indicating that the reminder shock-induced increase in freezing was derived from the original conditioned fear, not from new learning.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the control experiment showing that naive mice do not show high freezing to the reminder shock alone.

claim: The infralimbic cortex (IL) is a critical brain region for extinction.
source: Many studies have shown that the infralimbic cortex (IL) is a critical brain region for extinction (Herry et al., 2010; Sotres-Bayon and Quirk, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Extinction is suppressed by pharmacological inactivation of the IL.
source: Extinction is suppressed by pharmacological inactivation of the IL (Laurent and Westbrook, 2009; Sierra-Mercado et al., 2011) as well as by local injection of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) antagonists (Burgos-Robles et al., 2007; Sotres-Bayon et al., 2009) or cannabinoid antagonists (Lin et al., 2009) into the IL.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Extinction is suppressed by local injection of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) antagonists into the IL.
source: Extinction is suppressed by pharmacological inactivation of the IL (Laurent and Westbrook, 2009; Sierra-Mercado et al., 2011) as well as by local injection of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) antagonists (Burgos-Robles et al., 2007; Sotres-Bayon et al., 2009) or cannabinoid antagonists (Lin et al., 2009) into the IL.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Extinction is suppressed by local injection of cannabinoid antagonists into the IL.
source: Extinction is suppressed by pharmacological inactivation of the IL (Laurent and Westbrook, 2009; Sierra-Mercado et al., 2011) as well as by local injection of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) antagonists (Burgos-Robles et al., 2007; Sotres-Bayon et al., 2009) or cannabinoid antagonists (Lin et al., 2009) into the IL.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The IL inhibits the medial subdivision of the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeM), a key region for fear expression.
source: The IL inhibits the medial subdivision of the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeM), a key region for fear expression (Wilensky et al., 2006; Ciocchi et al., 2010), partly through intercalated amygdala neurons (ITCs) (Likhtik et al., 2008; Amano et al., 2010), which are also necessary for extinction.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The CeM is a key region for fear expression.
source: The IL inhibits the medial subdivision of the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeM), a key region for fear expression (Wilensky et al., 2006; Ciocchi et al., 2010), partly through intercalated amygdala neurons (ITCs) (Likhtik et al., 2008; Amano et al., 2010), which are also necessary for extinction.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The IL inhibits the CeM partly through intercalated amygdala neurons (ITCs).
source: The IL inhibits the medial subdivision of the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeM), a key region for fear expression (Wilensky et al., 2006; Ciocchi et al., 2010), partly through intercalated amygdala neurons (ITCs) (Likhtik et al., 2008; Amano et al., 2010), which are also necessary for extinction.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Intercalated amygdala neurons (ITCs) are necessary for extinction.
source: The IL inhibits the medial subdivision of the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeM), a key region for fear expression (Wilensky et al., 2006; Ciocchi et al., 2010), partly through intercalated amygdala neurons (ITCs) (Likhtik et al., 2008; Amano et al., 2010), which are also necessary for extinction.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: About 40% of patients in remission experience a relapse.
source: About 40% of patients in remission experience a relapse (Bruce et al., 2005; Ansell et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous clinical research.

claim: Fear can be reinstated by one or more US-only presentations after successful extinction.
source: In experimental animals, fear can be reinstated by one or more US-only presentations after successful extinction (Rescorla and Heth, 1975; Bertotto et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Fear reinstatement occurs through NMDAR- and protein synthesis-dependent neural plasticity.
source: We previously reported that fear reinstatement occurs through NMDAR- and protein synthesis-dependent neural plasticity (Shen et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Fear reinstatement requires β-adrenergic receptor activation, gamma-aminobutyric acid type A receptor endocytosis, and actin rearrangement in the basolateral amygdala (BLA).
source: It has also been reported that fear reinstatement requires β-adrenergic receptor activation, gamma-aminobutyric acid type A receptor endocytosis, and actin rearrangement in the basolateral amygdala (BLA) (Lin et al., 2011; Motanis and Maroun, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The BLA–medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) pathway is potentiated following fear extinction and depotentiated following reinstatement.
source: Interestingly, the BLA–medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) pathway is potentiated following fear extinction and depotentiated following reinstatement (Vouimba and Maroun, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The mPFC, amygdala, and hippocampus are important in fear modulation and have reciprocal connections.
source: We focused on the mPFC, amygdala, and hippocampus because they are important in fear modulation and have reciprocal connections (Quirk and Mueller, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Inactivation of the IL is sufficient to enhance fear responses.
source: Mice infused with muscimol showed higher freezing compared with those infused with a vehicle (Figure 1D), which is consistent with previous works in rats (Quirk et al., 2000; Laurent and Westbrook, 2009). These data suggest that inactivation of the IL is sufficient to enhance fear responses.
evidence: The claim is supported by the current experimental data and is consistent with cited previous research.

claim: Presynaptic depression in the IL is associated with reinstatement.
source: These results suggest that presynaptic depression in the IL is associated with reinstatement.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the electrophysiological data showing decreased mEPSC frequency and increased PPR in the Reinstatement group.

claim: The proportion of dopaminergic neurons among IL-projecting VTA neurons (59.1 ± 4.5%) is within the range reported in previous studies.
source: Of the retrogradely labelled cells (CTBIL+) in the VTA, 59.1 ± 4.5% were immunopositive for a dopamine neuron marker, tyrosine hydroxylase (TH+), indicating that they were dopaminergic. This is within the range reported in previous studies (Margolis et al., 2006; Lammel et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by the current data and comparison with cited previous research.

claim: A reminder shock activates dopaminergic VTA neurons projecting to the IL.
source: This result suggests that a reminder shock activates dopaminergic VTA neurons projecting to the IL.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the c-Fos expression data in IL-projecting dopaminergic VTA neurons.

claim: SCH23390 infusions into the prelimbic cortex (PL) did not affect reinstatement.
source: On the other hand, SCH23390 infusions into the prelimbic cortex (PL), a region adjacent to the IL, did not affect reinstatement (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from control experiments with PL infusions, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: IL dopaminergic signalling plays a specific role in the induction of reinstatement.
source: These results indicate a specific role of IL dopaminergic signalling in the induction of reinstatement.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the differential effects of D1R blockade in IL versus PL.

claim: IL D1R blockage attenuated reduction of synaptic input associated with reinstatement.
source: Thus, IL D1R blockage attenuated reduction of synaptic input associated with reinstatement.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the electrophysiological data showing that SCH23390 prevented the decrease in mEPSC frequency.

claim: IL D1R blockage prevents c-Fos expression changes in the amygdala associated with reinstatement.
source: Thus, we concluded that IL D1R blockage prevents c-Fos expression changes in the amygdala associated with reinstatement.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the immunohistochemistry data showing that SCH23390 prevented changes in ITCv and CeM c-Fos expression.

claim: D1R signalling in the IL is necessary for reduction of synaptic inputs, CeM disinhibition, and reinstatement.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that D1R signalling in the IL is necessary for reduction of synaptic inputs, CeM disinhibition, and reinstatement.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined results from behavioral, electrophysiological, and immunohistochemistry experiments with D1R blockade.

claim: A dopamine-dependent inactivation of extinction circuits underlies fear reinstatement.
source: These findings suggest that a dopamine-dependent inactivation of extinction circuits underlies fear reinstatement.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined results showing that dopamine signaling in the IL leads to reduced IL activity, decreased ITC activity, increased CeM activity, and fear reinstatement.

claim: Low IL activity may cause ITC downregulation and CeM upregulation to reinstate fear.
source: Low IL activity may cause ITC downregulation and CeM upregulation to reinstate fear.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observed pattern of c-Fos expression and known anatomical connections.

claim: Low activity of the IL and ITC could result in disinhibition of the CeM.
source: Therefore, low activity of the IL and ITC could result in disinhibition of the CeM.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on known anatomical connections and the observed c-Fos expression patterns.

claim: Disinhibition of the CeM by downregulation of IL–ITC pathway may underlie fear reinstatement.
source: Thus, disinhibition of the CeM by downregulation of IL–ITC pathway may underlie fear reinstatement.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observed c-Fos expression patterns and known circuit mechanisms.

claim: Aversive stimuli activate midbrain dopaminergic neurons.
source: Although it has also been reported that aversive stimuli activate midbrain dopaminergic neurons (Brischoux et al., 2009; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009), the exact role of dopamine released in aversive situations is poorly understood.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Dopamine neurons are activated in response to appetitive stimuli.
source: Many studies have shown that dopamine neurons are activated in response to appetitive stimuli, and that dopamine signalling affects reward-related behaviour and memory (Schultz, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Dopamine signalling affects reward-related behaviour and memory.
source: Many studies have shown that dopamine neurons are activated in response to appetitive stimuli, and that dopamine signalling affects reward-related behaviour and memory (Schultz, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Dopamine plays a critical role in reviving the aversive memory.
source: Moreover, blocking dopamine signalling in the IL prevented fear reinstatement (Figure 4A), suggesting the critical role of dopamine in reviving the aversive memory.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing that D1R blockade prevents reinstatement.

claim: VTA dopaminergic neurons that receive innervations from the lateral habenula preferentially project to the mPFC.
source: Anatomically, VTA dopaminergic neurons that receive innervations from the lateral habenula preferentially project to the mPFC (Lammel et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The habenula receives input from limbic system and this circuit is implicated in aversive information processing.
source: The habenula receives input from limbic system and this circuit is implicated in aversive information processing (Hikosaka, 2010; Okamoto et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It is possible that a reminder shock activates the habenula–VTA circuit and subsequent dopaminergic signalling in the IL.
source: Thus, it is possible that a reminder shock activates the habenula–VTA circuit and subsequent dopaminergic signalling in the IL.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on known anatomical connections and the current findings.

claim: Dopamine attenuates excitatory synaptic transmission in prefrontal neurons in a D1R-dependent manner.
source: Dopamine attenuates excitatory synaptic transmission in prefrontal neurons in a D1R-dependent manner (Gao et al., 2001; Mair and Kauer, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Application of dopamine, combined with electrical stimulation, can induce long-term synaptic depression in the mPFC.
source: Application of dopamine, combined with electrical stimulation, can induce long-term synaptic depression in the mPFC (Law-Tho et al., 1995; Huang et al., 2004); however, the phenomenon is not observed in heterozygous D1R knockout mice (Huang et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Dopamine-induced long-term synaptic depression in the mPFC is not observed in heterozygous D1R knockout mice.
source: Application of dopamine, combined with electrical stimulation, can induce long-term synaptic depression in the mPFC (Law-Tho et al., 1995; Huang et al., 2004); however, the phenomenon is not observed in heterozygous D1R knockout mice (Huang et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: One possible mechanism for dopamine-mediated presynaptic depression is that dopamine triggers adenosine release and subsequently activates presynaptic adenosine A1 receptors.
source: One possible mechanism is that dopamine triggers adenosine release and subsequently activates presynaptic adenosine A1 receptors.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: D1Rs and adenosine-mediated presynaptic depression have been reported in the VTA of guinea pigs.
source: D1Rs and adenosine-mediated presynaptic depression have also been reported in the VTA of guinea pigs (Bonci and Williams, 1996) and in the basal ganglia of zebra finches (Ding et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: D1Rs and adenosine-mediated presynaptic depression have been reported in the basal ganglia of zebra finches.
source: D1Rs and adenosine-mediated presynaptic depression have also been reported in the VTA of guinea pigs (Bonci and Williams, 1996) and in the basal ganglia of zebra finches (Ding et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A reminder shock activates VTA dopaminergic neurons projecting to the IL, and dopamine D1R signalling lowers IL activity with presynaptic depression, which could result in low activity of the ventral ITC, thereby disinhibiting CeM and reinstating a once extinguished fear.
source: The present findings suggest a possible dopaminergic mechanism of fear reinstatement as follows: a reminder shock activates VTA dopaminergic neurons projecting to the IL, and dopamine D1R signalling lowers IL activity with presynaptic depression, which could result in low activity of the ventral ITC, thereby disinhibiting CeM and reinstating a once extinguished fear.
evidence: The claim is a synthesis and interpretation of the experimental findings, representing a proposed mechanism.

claim: Drugs of abuse increase dopamine release in both animals and humans.
source: Previous studies have shown that drugs of abuse increase dopamine release in both animals (Di Chiara and Imperato, 1988; Chen et al., 1990) and humans (Laruelle et al., 1995; Volkow et al., 1999; Drevets et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The dopaminergic mechanism of reinstatement may explain the high rate of comorbid substance use disorders with anxiety disorders.
source: This dopaminergic mechanism of reinstatement may explain the high rate of comorbid substance use disorders with anxiety disorders (Kendler et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is a speculation about clinical implications, supported by citation to epidemiological research.

claim: There is a high rate of comorbid substance use disorders with anxiety disorders.
source: This dopaminergic mechanism of reinstatement may explain the high rate of comorbid substance use disorders with anxiety disorders (Kendler et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Activity mapping with c-Fos is a well-established and often used method to identify brain regions that are involved in processing motivation behaviour, social behaviour, learning and memory.
source: Activity mapping with c-Fos is a well-established and often used method to identify brain regions that are involved in processing motivation behaviour, social behaviour, learning and memory, and so on (Zhang and Kelley, 2000; Tronel and Sara, 2002; Frankland et al., 2004; Veening et al., 2005; Makino et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neuronal activation patterns detected by c-Fos expression and by functional magnetic resonance imaging correlate well.
source: Other studies reporting that neuronal activation patterns detected by c-Fos expression and by functional magnetic resonance imaging correlate well (Lu et al., 2004; Lazovic et al., 2005) also support the utility of c-Fos immunohistochemistry to determine changes in neuronal activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: c-Fos expression is dependent on an increase in Ca2+.
source: Because c-Fos expression is dependent on an increase in Ca2+ (Lerea et al., 1992), firing activity does not always result in c-Fos elevation (Clayton, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Firing activity does not always result in c-Fos elevation.
source: Because c-Fos expression is dependent on an increase in Ca2+ (Lerea et al., 1992), firing activity does not always result in c-Fos elevation (Clayton, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The PL promotes fear responses.
source: The PL promotes fear responses.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the role of the PL in fear.

claim: Neuronal activity of the PL, which is elevated during fear retrieval, is not elevated (or lowered) during extinction retrieval.
source: As indicated by our data and previous reports, neuronal activity of the PL, which is elevated during fear retrieval, is not elevated (or lowered) during extinction retrieval (Burgos-Robles et al., 2009; Sotres-Bayon et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by the current data and citations to previous research.

claim: The IL increases its activity during extinction retrieval.
source: On the other hand, the IL increases its activity during extinction retrieval (Milad and Quirk, 2002), suggesting the negative control of fear expression by the IL.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The IL negatively controls fear expression.
source: On the other hand, the IL increases its activity during extinction retrieval (Milad and Quirk, 2002), suggesting the negative control of fear expression by the IL.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on cited research showing IL activity during extinction retrieval.

claim: Fear reinstatement is regulated by downregulation of extinction circuits.
source: Our findings suggest that fear reinstatement is regulated by downregulation of extinction circuits.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed pattern of c-Fos expression showing decreased IL activity during reinstatement.

claim: The IL has direct projections to the ITC.
source: The IL has direct projections to the ITC (Cho et al., 2013), which is critically involved in fear extinction (Likhtik et al., 2008; Busti et al., 2011; Mańko et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The ITC is critically involved in fear extinction.
source: The IL has direct projections to the ITC (Cho et al., 2013), which is critically involved in fear extinction (Likhtik et al., 2008; Busti et al., 2011; Mańko et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The ITC provides feedforward inhibition of output neurons in the CeM.
source: The ITC provides feedforward inhibition of output neurons in the CeM (Royer et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The CeM projects to brain structures controlling conditioned fear responses, including the periaqueductal grey and the ventromedial and lateral hypothalamus.
source: The CeM projects to brain structures controlling conditioned fear responses, including the periaqueductal grey and the ventromedial and lateral hypothalamus (Hopkins and Holstege, 1978; Veening et al., 1984; Cassell et al., 1986), and CeM activity is necessary and sufficient for expression of freezing (Wilensky et al., 2006; Ciocchi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CeM activity is necessary and sufficient for expression of freezing.
source: The CeM projects to brain structures controlling conditioned fear responses, including the periaqueductal grey and the ventromedial and lateral hypothalamus (Hopkins and Holstege, 1978; Veening et al., 1984; Cassell et al., 1986), and CeM activity is necessary and sufficient for expression of freezing (Wilensky et al., 2006; Ciocchi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The lateral subdivision of the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeL) receives projections from the IL.
source: Another possible pathway is through the lateral subdivision of the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeL), which also receives projections from the IL and contains two functionally distinct subpopulations of neurons (CElon or somatostatin-expressing neurons, and CEloff or protein kinase C-δ-expressing neurons) forming local inhibitory circuits to inhibit CeM activity (Ciocchi et al., 2010; Haubensak et al., 2010; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The CeL contains two functionally distinct subpopulations of neurons (CElon or somatostatin-expressing neurons, and CEloff or protein kinase C-δ-expressing neurons) forming local inhibitory circuits to inhibit CeM activity.
source: Another possible pathway is through the lateral subdivision of the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeL), which also receives projections from the IL and contains two functionally distinct subpopulations of neurons (CElon or somatostatin-expressing neurons, and CEloff or protein kinase C-δ-expressing neurons) forming local inhibitory circuits to inhibit CeM activity (Ciocchi et al., 2010; Haubensak et al., 2010; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The mPFC, including the IL, receives dopaminergic innervation from the ventral tegmental area (VTA).
source: The mPFC, including the IL, receives dopaminergic innervation from the ventral tegmental area (VTA).
evidence: The claim is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Aversive stimuli activate VTA dopaminergic neurons.
source: It is reported that aversive stimuli activate VTA dopaminergic neurons (Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009; Brischoux et al., 2009) and elevate dopamine concentration in the PFC (Abercrombie et al., 1989; Hamamura and Fibiger, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Aversive stimuli elevate dopamine concentration in the PFC.
source: It is reported that aversive stimuli activate VTA dopaminergic neurons (Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009; Brischoux et al., 2009) and elevate dopamine concentration in the PFC (Abercrombie et al., 1989; Hamamura and Fibiger, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Dopamine application with electric stimulation suppresses transmitter release onto mPFC neurons via dopamine D1 receptors (D1Rs).
source: Additionally, dopamine application with electric stimulation suppresses transmitter release onto mPFC neurons via dopamine D1 receptors (D1Rs) (Law-Tho et al., 1994; Gao et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Anxiety disorders are often treated with cognitive-behavioural interventions such as exposure therapy.
source: Anxiety disorders are often treated with cognitive-behavioural interventions such as exposure therapy (McNally, 2007; Vervliet et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Fear conditioning and extinction are used in animal models of anxiety disorders and their treatment.
source: Fear conditioning and extinction are used in animal models of anxiety disorders and their treatment (Davis, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In extinction, conditioned responses can be reduced by prolonged presentations of conditional stimuli (CS) without the associated unconditional stimuli (US).
source: In extinction, conditioned responses can be reduced by prolonged presentations of conditional stimuli (CS) without the associated unconditional stimuli (US) (LeDoux, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Prevention of relapses is a major challenge in treating anxiety disorders.
source: Prevention of relapses is a major challenge in treating anxiety disorders.
evidence: The claim is based on established clinical knowledge.

claim: Fear reinstatement can cause relapse in spite of successful fear reduction through extinction-based exposure therapy.
source: Fear reinstatement can cause relapse in spite of successful fear reduction through extinction-based exposure therapy.
evidence: The claim is based on established clinical and experimental knowledge.

claim: Reinstatement was accompanied by decreased c-Fos expression in the infralimbic cortex (IL) with reduction of synaptic input.
source: By utilising a contextual fear-conditioning task in mice, we found that reinstatement was accompanied by decreased c-Fos expression in the infralimbic cortex (IL) with reduction of synaptic input and enhanced c-Fos expression in the medial subdivision of the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeM).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from c-Fos immunohistochemistry and electrophysiology experiments.

claim: Reinstatement was accompanied by enhanced c-Fos expression in the medial subdivision of the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeM).
source: By utilising a contextual fear-conditioning task in mice, we found that reinstatement was accompanied by decreased c-Fos expression in the infralimbic cortex (IL) with reduction of synaptic input and enhanced c-Fos expression in the medial subdivision of the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeM).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from c-Fos immunohistochemistry.

claim: IL dopamine plays a key role in reinstatement.
source: Moreover, we found that IL dopamine plays a key role in reinstatement.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing that D1R blockade prevents reinstatement.

claim: A reinstatement-inducing reminder shock induced c-Fos expression in the IL-projecting dopaminergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area.
source: A reinstatement-inducing reminder shock induced c-Fos expression in the IL-projecting dopaminergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area, and the blocking of IL D1 signalling prevented reduction of synaptic input, CeM c-Fos expression, and fear reinstatement.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from retrograde tracing and c-Fos immunohistochemistry.

claim: The blocking of IL D1 signalling prevented reduction of synaptic input.
source: A reinstatement-inducing reminder shock induced c-Fos expression in the IL-projecting dopaminergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area, and the blocking of IL D1 signalling prevented reduction of synaptic input, CeM c-Fos expression, and fear reinstatement.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from electrophysiology experiments with D1R antagonist.

claim: The blocking of IL D1 signalling prevented CeM c-Fos expression.
source: A reinstatement-inducing reminder shock induced c-Fos expression in the IL-projecting dopaminergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area, and the blocking of IL D1 signalling prevented reduction of synaptic input, CeM c-Fos expression, and fear reinstatement.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from c-Fos immunohistochemistry with D1R antagonist.

claim: The blocking of IL D1 signalling prevented fear reinstatement.
source: A reinstatement-inducing reminder shock induced c-Fos expression in the IL-projecting dopaminergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area, and the blocking of IL D1 signalling prevented reduction of synaptic input, CeM c-Fos expression, and fear reinstatement.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from behavioral experiments with D1R antagonist.

claim: The dopaminergic mechanism of reinstatement may explain the comorbidity of substance use disorders and anxiety disorders.
source: These findings demonstrate that a dopamine-dependent inactivation of extinction circuits underlies fear reinstatement and may explain the comorbidity of substance use disorders and anxiety disorders.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about clinical implications based on the experimental findings.

claim: The maximum number of action potentials in the Reinstatement group was not significantly different from either the Extinction group or the Fear group.
source: The maximum number of action potentials in the Reinstatement group was not significantly different from either the Extinction group or the Fear group, while that of the Extinction group was higher than that of the Fear group, consistent with a previous study using auditory fear conditioning (Santini et al., 2008) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data measuring intrinsic excitability.

claim: The maximum number of action potentials of the Extinction group was higher than that of the Fear group, consistent with a previous study using auditory fear conditioning.
source: The maximum number of action potentials in the Reinstatement group was not significantly different from either the Extinction group or the Fear group, while that of the Extinction group was higher than that of the Fear group, consistent with a previous study using auditory fear conditioning (Santini et al., 2008) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the current electrophysiological data and citation to previous research.

claim: Intrinsic excitability of IL neurons did not change with fear reinstatement.
source: Thus, intrinsic excitability of IL neurons did not change with fear reinstatement.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the electrophysiological data showing no change in maximum number of action potentials.

claim: Excitatory synaptic inputs to the IL were decreased with reinstatement.
source: Frequency of miniature excitatory postsynaptic current (mEPSC) was lower in the Reinstatement group than it was in the Extinction group (Figure 2A,B), while mEPSC amplitude was comparable across groups (Figure 2C). Thus, excitatory synaptic inputs to the IL were decreased with reinstatement.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the electrophysiological data showing decreased mEPSC frequency.

claim: Increased PPR in the Reinstatement group indicates decreased transmitter release to IL neurons.
source: PPR was higher in the Reinstatement group than it was in the Extinction group (Figure 2E,F), indicating decreased transmitter release to IL neurons.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the electrophysiological data showing increased PPR, which is a standard measure of release probability.

claim: There were no significant differences between the Extinction and Reinstatement groups in other sub-regions of the mPFC, amygdala, or hippocampus.
source: There were no significant differences between the Extinction and Reinstatement groups in other sub-regions of the mPFC, amygdala, or hippocampus (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data from multiple brain regions, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Low IL activity disinhibits the CeM during fear reinstatement.
source: These results suggest that low IL activity disinhibits the CeM during fear reinstatement.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the c-Fos expression patterns and known circuit connections.

claim: All experiments were approved by the animal experiment ethics committee at The University of Tokyo (approval number 24-10).
source: All experiments were approved by the animal experiment ethics committee at The University of Tokyo (approval number 24-10) and were in accordance with The University of Tokyo guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals.
evidence: The claim is a statement of ethical approval for the research.

claim: Male C57BL/6J mice (8–15 weeks old) were used in the experiments.
source: Male C57BL/6J mice (8–15 weeks old; SLC, Shizuoka, Japan) were housed in group cages of four under standard laboratory conditions (12-hr light/12-hr dark cycle, with light from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. and free access to food and water).
evidence: The claim is a description of the experimental subjects.
